elements.text: How did they raise stone that high?
And why, sometimes, did it come down?

shot.narration: The people who built them had no knowledge of material properties or allowable stresses. So how did they raise stone that high? And why, sometimes, did it come down?
shot.visual_purpose: Title card: the central question [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (5 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (5 elements)

elements.text: Pulled apart: little or no strength

shot.narration: Start with the stone itself. Stone has little or no strength when it is pulled apart. So a stone building has to stand by keeping its stones pressed together.
shot.visual_purpose: An arch of wedge-shaped stones: pressed together, not pulled apart [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (20 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (20 elements)

shot.narration: Gothic builders took a different approach. They stopped fighting thrust with sheer thickness, and learned to channel it. Three tools made that possible: the pointed arch, the rib vault, and the flying buttress.
shot.visual_purpose: The three tools named as they are spoken [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (11 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (11 elements)

elements.text: Conceptual arrows: direction only, not calculated

shot.narration: A pointed arch is two arcs of a circle that meet at a point. Compared with a round arch, it pushes less to the sides, and that lets it rise much higher.
shot.visual_purpose: Round and pointed arch on the same span; the push turns downward [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (10 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (10 elements)

elements.text: “As hangs the flexible line, so but inverted
will stand the rigid arch.”  Robert Hooke, 1675

shot.narration: In 1675, the scientist Robert Hooke summed up the shape of a good arch in one line. As hangs the flexible line, so but inverted will stand the rigid arch. In other words, the force in an arch follows a curve like a hanging chain, turned upside down. A Columbia University project says the pointed arch comes closer to that curve than the round arch, and so is more efficient.
shot.visual_purpose: Hanging chain, inverted, beside a pointed arch [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (12 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (12 elements)

shot.narration: The pointed arch was not a Gothic invention. It already appears in Burgundy, at the rebuilding of the abbey of Cluny around 1088, and the same Columbia project traces it to Islamic sources. At the abbey of Saint-Denis, it was used systematically, together with the other new ideas.
shot.visual_purpose: Short timeline: pointed arches before Gothic [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (18 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (18 elements)

elements.text: Wide bay, narrow bay: conceptual diagram

shot.narration: It had a subtler advantage too. Unlike a round arch, a pointed arch can span sections of different widths, called bays, and still reach the same height at its crown. That was a valuable asset for keeping complex vaults regular.
shot.visual_purpose: Level crowns over different widths [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (11 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (11 elements)

shot.narration: The second tool is the rib vault. Two pointed arches cross diagonally over each bay of the building. They gather the vault's load onto four points: the piers, or stone pillars, at its corners.
shot.visual_purpose: Plan of one bay: ribs to four piers [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (11 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (11 elements)

shot.narration: Ribs were not new either. They appear at Durham Cathedral, in England, as early as 1093, and Columbia's project traces them to Islamic, Roman and Byzantine sources.
shot.visual_purpose: The same timeline, with ribbed vaults added [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (21 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (21 elements)

shot.narration: Why go to all this trouble? Part of the answer is light. At the abbey church of Saint-Denis, Abbot Suger built a new choir between 1140 and 1144. Pointed arches run throughout, every vault is ribbed, and monumental stained glass seems to dissolve the whole structure.
shot.visual_purpose: Saint-Denis, dates and three features (a rights-cleared photograph may replace the card) [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (23 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (23 elements)

elements.text: “A sign or bridge to the divine”
The new style had to let in as much light as possible

shot.narration: For Suger, light was a sign, a bridge to the divine. France's national library says the new style had to let in as much light as possible.
shot.visual_purpose: Why light mattered [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (3 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (3 elements)

elements.text: of stained glass at Chartres, most of it original

shot.narration: At Chartres, some 2,500 square meters of stained glass survive, most of it original.
shot.visual_purpose: One number (a rights-cleared photograph of the glass may replace the card) [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (2 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (2 elements)

elements.text: Suger's crypt: round arches, groin vaults

shot.narration: How new was all of this? On that question, historians still disagree. Following the 19th-century architect Viollet-le-Duc, some call Gothic an entire revolution in the art of building. The art historian Arnaud Timbert argues there was no revolution and no Gothic break, but a creative proposal rooted in continuity. Suger's own crypt still relies almost entirely on round arches and groin vaults.
shot.visual_purpose: Two readings, side by side [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (9 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (9 elements)

shot.narration: So how did they do all this, with no knowledge of material properties? Master builders used geometrical rules, developed through centuries of trial and error. They scaled up the same proportions for new, larger elements.
shot.visual_purpose: One proportion at three sizes [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (6 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (6 elements)

shot.narration: At Amiens, setting out the site began with ropes pegged to the ground. Squares with perfect right angles controlled the plan, and templates for piers, windows and vaults were designed with straight-edge and compass.
shot.visual_purpose: Ropes, pegs and a square turned inside a square [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (10 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (10 elements)

elements.text: Each cut to a wooden template

shot.narration: Arches were usually drawn full size on the ground, then divided into wedge-shaped stones called voussoirs. Each voussoir was cut to a wooden template, and the stones were laid on a rigid wooden frame called centering. The frame came away only once the mortar had set: at Amiens, after a couple of months or so.
shot.visual_purpose: An arch on centering; the centering goes away [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (29 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (29 elements)

elements.text: Ties stopped the arches pushing the upper piers over

shot.narration: Carpenters built the scaffolding, the formwork for the vaults and the lifting gear. They also tied the upper piers with wood, and later iron, to stop the arches pushing them over.
shot.visual_purpose: What the carpenters made (words, no workers or machinery) [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (6 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (6 elements)

shot.narration: All of this took generations of work. The foundation stone of Amiens was laid in 1220, and its main roof was not finished until about 1310.
shot.visual_purpose: Ninety years on one line [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (17 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (17 elements)

elements.text: A fire damages the old Romanesque choir
The bishop rebuilds, after the greatest buildings of his time

shot.narration: Which brings us back to Beauvais. In 1225, a fire damaged the old Romanesque choir, and the bishop decided to rebuild it, inspired by the greatest buildings of his time.
shot.visual_purpose: Place and date [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (4 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (4 elements)

shot.narration: By the 1250s, the two lower levels of the new choir were finished. Then the bishop apparently decided to go beyond the planned proportions, adding about five meters to the upper windows, and so to the vaults. By 1272, the clergy could use the new choir.
shot.visual_purpose: Three levels; the top one grows [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (12 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (12 elements)

elements.text: The highest vaults of the Middle Ages

shot.narration: Its vault rose nearly 47 meters, a few meters above Amiens. These were the highest vaults built in the Middle Ages.
shot.visual_purpose: Two heights side by side, with the caveat on screen [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (9 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (9 elements)

elements.text: Why did the vaults fall? Still debated.
Settling masonry broke the flying buttresses
Gusts of wind set the buttress system resonating
2024 study: nothing justifies a foundation cause
Vaults raised against proven proportions: upper parts too flexible

shot.narration: Why it happened is still debated. Some blame settling masonry that broke the flying buttresses. Others point to gusts of wind setting the buttress system resonating, or to slow settlement of the foundations. A 2024 study found nothing to justify a foundation cause. Its authors argue that raising the vaults, against proven proportions, left the upper parts too flexible.
shot.visual_purpose: The explanations, one by one [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (8 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (8 elements)

elements.text: Longer to repair than to build (Stephen Murray)

shot.narration: The repair tells its own story. New piers went up between the old ones, turning three bays into six. The work was not finished until 1340: as the historian Stephen Murray put it, it took longer to repair the choir than to build it.
shot.visual_purpose: Plan of the choir's straight bays: three become six [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (19 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (19 elements)

elements.text: Four slender piers, no support to the west
The great Gothic nave: never built

shot.narration: In the sixteenth century, work began again, with a new transept, the cross-arm of the building. Then, instead of a nave, the builders raised a lantern tower and spire about 150 meters high, finished in 1569. It rested on four slender piers, and the sources point to a lack of support on the west side, where the nave had not been built. In 1573, just four years after it was finished, the tower came down. The great Gothic nave was never built.
shot.visual_purpose: Timeline; the fall is told, not shown [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (20 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (20 elements)

elements.text: Within two centuries, the crossing piers were threatening collapse

shot.narration: Beauvais was not alone. At Amiens, within two centuries, the piers at the crossing, where the arms of the building meet, were threatening collapse. Between 1497 and 1500, an iron chain was installed to stop the movement, and it still runs through the building today.
shot.visual_purpose: Two piers tied by a chain [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (7 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (7 elements)

elements.text: Line of thrust inside the stone

shot.narration: Picture the path of the force through the stone, which engineers call the line of thrust. As long as that line can stay inside the masonry, the structure can stand in compression. If no such line can be found, it collapses.
shot.visual_purpose: The line of thrust inside an arch; a line that no longer fits [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (33 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (33 elements)

elements.text: Rules of geometry, learned by trial and error

shot.narration: What matters most, then, is shape and proportion. Stability, unlike some other engineering problems, can be scaled: a model with the same proportions is a good guide to the stability of the real building. That helps explain how rules of geometry, learned by trial and error, could carry builders so far.
shot.visual_purpose: One shape at two sizes [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (6 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (6 elements)

elements.text: Not a simple story of progress
Saint-Denis: a bright choir over a crypt of older forms

shot.narration: But it is not a simple story of progress. Beauvais needed new piers, Amiens needed an iron chain, and Suger's bright choir rose above a crypt of older forms. Each cathedral was a test in stone, built by people who learned from centuries of trial and error.
shot.visual_purpose: Not a linear progression [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (5 elements)]

shots.explanation: 2D card supplied by the beat (5 elements)

shot.narration: Which building or structure should we explain next? Suggest a topic in the comments. And if you enjoyed this film, please like it and subscribe.

coverage.narration: The answer stands outside the building: the flying buttress. It is a stone arch that picks up the thrust where it leaves the vault, carries it across the aisle roof, and brings it down to a massive pier buttress. Often a pinnacle on top adds weight, to help stabilize the thrust.

coverage.narration: One way to picture it comes from Columbia's Amiens project. It is as if the thick outer wall had been cut into segments, and each segment turned 90 degrees. Those segments become rigid supports, standing out from the building, with exposed arches reaching up to the high vaults.

coverage.narration: According to France's national library, the first flying buttresses were used to consolidate Romanesque churches that threatened to collapse. It also says that the slanting timber props used while building the vaults were, in effect, made permanent in stone. At Chartres, flying buttresses were part of the original plans. And around the east end of Notre-Dame in Paris, they look almost like a giant external skeleton.
